title: A $750,000 Horror Film Just Took Over Mumbai's Regal Cinema. Anurag Kashyap Wants to Know Why.
excerpt: Obsession has crossed ₹70 crore in India, stealing screens from Bollywood's biggest names — and one of the industry's most respected directors just went public with his frustration.
body:
Here is a sentence that should terrify every Hindi film producer reading this: Obsession, a Hollywood horror movie that cost less to make than a single Bollywood song shoot, is now the highest-grossing film in Indian theaters this weekend. Not the highest-grossing horror film. Not the highest-grossing Hollywood film. The highest-grossing film, period — beating every single new Bollywood release that opened against it.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=4E0-K9F16r8

And Anurag Kashyap has had enough.

The Numbers That Started a War

Let's rewind. Obsession opened in India on May 29 with ₹1.60 crore on Day 1. A modest number for a Hollywood genre film with no A-list stars — Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette are not exactly household names in Mumbai. The film was directed by Curry Barker, produced on a micro-budget of roughly $750,000, and positioned as a mid-tier horror release.

Then word of mouth hit.

By its second weekend, the film was collecting ₹8.75 crore on a single Sunday — more than five times its opening day. Its second weekend total of ₹20.75 crore nearly matched its entire first week. The kind of trajectory you see once every few years. By its third Saturday — yesterday — it crossed the ₹70 crore mark in India, with a projected lifetime north of ₹100 crore. That would make it the biggest Hollywood film of 2026 in India, surpassing both Project Hail Mary and The Conjuring: Last Rites.

The audience has spoken. The problem is what that speech is costing everyone else.

Regal Falls

On Friday, June 12, four Bollywood films opened simultaneously: Main Vaapas Aaunga (Imtiaz Ali's partition drama starring Diljit Dosanjh), Bharat Bhhagya Viddhaata (Kangana Ranaut's 26/11 film), Haunted 3D: Echoes of the Past, and Governor (starring Manoj Bajpayee). A packed, competitive weekend.

By Saturday, Mumbai's iconic Regal Cinema — one of the city's oldest single screens, a venue that has premiered some of India's greatest films — quietly pulled both Main Vaapas Aaunga and Bharat Bhhagya Viddhaata from its schedule. In their place: four shows of Obsession. Not because anyone forced them to. Because that's where the money was.

Kangana's film collected ₹1 crore on opening day — with a Buy-One-Get-One ticket offer. Without the BOGO, the real number would have been even lower. The film is tracking toward a ₹4-4.50 crore opening weekend, a result even the trade is calling "disastrous." Imtiaz Ali's Main Vaapas Aaunga, despite strong critical praise and an A.R. Rahman score, managed roughly ₹61 lakh in advance booking across national chains.

Meanwhile, Obsession collected ₹7 crore on Saturday alone. In its third week.

"I Don't Understand How We Will Grow"

Enter Anurag Kashyap. The director of Gangs of Wasseypur, Dev.D, and Sacred Games — and the man whose latest film Bandar (starring Bobby Deol) earned just ₹4 crore in its entire run — took to Instagram Stories to lay it bare.

"I totally understand that everyone wants to see OBSESSION, but it can still run longer with lesser shows. If we don't prioritise our own films with better showcasing then I don't understand how will we grow. Last week it was with BANDAR, this week with MAIN VAPIS AUNGA, SING GHEETAM and GOVERNER. We have one morning show of MVA and maybe another in some cinemas and same with GOVERNER and no show of SING GHEETAM in Bengaluru. While OBSESSION IS IN 6-7 shows." — Anurag Kashyap

He's not wrong about the math. A single screen running Obsession in 6-7 daily shows leaves Indian films fighting for one early-morning slot — the graveyard shift of cinema exhibition. For mid-budget Indian films without the marketing muscle of a YRF or Dharma, it's a death sentence disguised as programming.

What This Means for NRI Viewers

If you're in the US, UK, or Canada, you've likely already seen Obsession — the film has crossed $224 million worldwide and dominated North American screens for weeks. But the Indian box office story matters to diaspora audiences for a different reason.

The films being squeezed off screens — Main Vaapas Aaunga, Governor, Bandar — are exactly the kind of mid-range, director-driven Indian cinema that NRIs often discover on streaming weeks later and wish they'd caught in theaters. Kashyap's frustration isn't just about his own film. It's about whether the Indian theatrical ecosystem can sustain anything that isn't either a franchise blockbuster or a global horror phenomenon.

Bollywood's crucial summer window — Cocktail 2 (June 19), Welcome to the Jungle (June 26), Alpha (July 3), Dhamaal 4 (July 10) — is about to collide head-on with a film that refuses to slow down. Whether those releases have the star power to reclaim screens remains the industry's biggest open question.

For now, Georgekutty isn't the only one running out of hiding places.
